geothermal-s1.title: Heating one home for a year: furnace or heat pump

table.caption: Energy used and prices for heating the same house for one winter (invented data for practice)

geothermal-s1.text: A therm is a unit of heat energy used for natural gas (1 therm = 100,000 BTU).

geothermal-s2.title: Geothermal power plant and ground source heat pump

items.q: Where does geothermal energy come from?
options: Sunlight that warms the soil
Natural gas burned underground
Friction from flowing water
Heat from Earth's interior

why.correct: Geothermal heat comes mostly from radioactive decay deep in Earth, plus heat left over from Earth's formation.
options: Sunlight warms only the top few meters; geothermal plants tap heat from far deeper.
No fuel is burned in a geothermal plant.
Water flow does not make meaningful heat.
Right: heat from Earth's interior.

items.q: Why are geothermal power plants built in places like Iceland, New Zealand and California but rarely in the middle of continents?
options: Geothermal plants have to be built next to an ocean for cooling
The middle of a continent has no heat at any depth beneath it
Hot rock is near the surface at plate boundaries
Those places get more sunlight to heat the ground than other places

why.correct: Making electricity needs very hot water or steam at depths that can be drilled. That happens near plate boundaries, hot spots and volcanic areas.
options: Coastal cooling is not the reason.
Heat exists everywhere at depth; it is just too deep to reach cheaply in most places.
Right: plate boundaries bring heat near the surface.
Geothermal heat comes from below, not from sunlight.

items.q: At a geothermal power plant, why is the cooled water pumped back down into the ground?
options: To cool the hot rock so that the plant can shut down
To refill the underground reservoir
To add more salt to the water so that it boils faster
To store the plant's electricity as heat for later use

why.correct: Injecting the water back keeps the reservoir from running dry and disposes of water that may carry dissolved minerals.
options: The goal is to keep the plant running, not to cool the rock.
Right: reinjection keeps the resource from being depleted.
Adding salt is not the purpose.
Electricity is not stored this way.

items.q: A geothermal field produced less steam each year after its wells were drilled. What is the most likely cause?
options: Hot water was removed faster than it returned
Earth's core has started to cool down quickly in that region
Sunlight on the field was blocked by new buildings nearby
The steam was used up by radioactive decay deep underground

why.correct: A geothermal reservoir can be depleted if hot water is withdrawn faster than it is recharged, which is why plants reinject water.
options: Right: overuse can deplete a geothermal reservoir.
Earth's interior cools far too slowly to matter.
Sunlight does not drive geothermal steam.
Radioactive decay makes heat; it does not use up steam.

items.q: How does a ground source heat pump heat a house in winter?
options: It burns natural gas that is stored in the soil
It uses sunlight that is stored in the roof shingles
It makes electricity from hot steam under the house
It moves heat from the ground into the house

why.correct: A few meters down, the ground stays about 10 to 16 °C all year. Fluid in buried pipes picks up that heat, and the heat pump concentrates it into the house.
options: No fuel is burned.
Roof sunlight is solar energy, not a heat pump.
Heat pumps work with mild ground temperatures, not steam.
Right: the pump moves heat from the ground into the house.

items.q: Why can a ground source heat pump work almost anywhere, unlike a geothermal power plant?
options: It burns fuel, so it does not depend on the ground beneath it
It runs on the wind that blows across the open ground
Shallow ground has a steady temperature nearly everywhere
It needs water hotter than 150 °C, found under most houses

why.correct: Heat pumps need only the steady temperature of shallow ground, not hot rock near the surface. They do need electricity to run the pump.
options: A heat pump burns no fuel; it uses electricity to move heat.
Wind is not involved.
Right: shallow ground is a steady temperature almost everywhere.
Such hot water is found only in volcanic areas.

items.q: Which is an environmental drawback of some geothermal power plants?
options: They flood large river valleys behind tall dams
They can release hydrogen sulfide gas
They release large amounts of soot, just like a coal plant
They depend on daylight and stop working each night

why.correct: Underground steam can carry hydrogen sulfide and small amounts of carbon dioxide and dissolved minerals. Releases are far smaller than from fossil fuel plants.
options: Flooding valleys is a dam's impact.
Right: hydrogen sulfide and some dissolved minerals.
Geothermal plants burn nothing, so they make no soot.
Geothermal runs day and night.

items.q: Write the setup for the yearly cost of heating the home with the natural gas furnace, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Dividing by the price leaves therms squared per dollar. Multiply therms by dollars per therm.
You divided by the price. Multiply the therms used by the price per therm.

items.q: What is the yearly cost of heating the home with the ground source heat pump?

mistakes.why: You used the gas price per therm. The heat pump runs on electricity at \$0.14 per kWh.
You divided by the price. Multiply kWh by dollars per kWh.

items.q: The heat pump costs \$12,000 more to install than a new furnace. Write the setup for the number of years for the yearly savings to repay that extra cost, then give the answer.

why.correct: Yearly savings: $1{,}040 - 924 = 116$ dollars. Payback: $\frac{12{,}000}{1{,}040 - 924} \approx 103$ years. At these prices the heat pump does not pay for itself in its lifetime; it is chosen to cut emissions, or where gas is costlier.

mistakes.why: Put brackets around the difference: 12,000 ÷ (1,040 - 924). Without them the division happens first.
Divide by the yearly savings (1,040 - 924), not by the heat pump's cost.
You divided by the heat pump's yearly cost. Divide by the yearly savings, 1,040 - 924 = 116 dollars.

items.q: The local utility makes its electricity from wind and sunlight. Which conclusion about the two heating systems is best supported?
options: The heat pump would release carbon dioxide stored in the ground
The heat pump would cut heating emissions sharply
The furnace would release less carbon dioxide than the heat pump
Both systems would release the same amount of carbon dioxide

why.correct: The furnace burns natural gas in the home; the heat pump runs on electricity, which here comes from sources that release no carbon dioxide while running.
options: The ground loop moves heat; it does not release gas.
Right: clean electricity makes the heat pump nearly emission-free in use.
The furnace burns gas, which releases carbon dioxide.
One burns gas; the other uses clean electricity.

items.q: In the power plant on the left of the diagram, what spins the turbine?
options: Steam from the production well
Cooled water in the injection well
Burning fuel in a boiler
Wind blowing across the surface

why.correct: Steam and hot water rise up the production well and spin the turbine.
options: Right: steam from underground.
The injection well returns water after it has done its work.
Nothing is burned.
Wind is not part of the diagram.

items.q: On the right of the diagram, why does the heat pump move heat into the house in winter but out of it in summer?
options: The ground heats up in winter and cools in summer
The house makes its own heat in winter from the pipes
The pump runs on sunlight, which changes with the season
The ground is warmer than winter air and cooler than summer air

why.correct: A few meters down, the ground stays about the same temperature all year: warmer than the winter air, cooler than the summer air.
options: The ground's temperature stays nearly steady.
The pipes carry heat from the ground; they do not make it.
The pump runs on electricity.
Right: the ground's steady temperature is between winter and summer air.

items.q: Both systems in the diagram use heat from the ground. Which statement compares them correctly?
options: The heat pump makes electricity and the power plant makes heat
Neither one uses electricity or fuel to run
Only the plant needs hot rock near the surface
Both need hot rock near a plate boundary to work

why.correct: The power plant needs very hot water or steam, found near plate boundaries. The heat pump needs only the mild, steady temperature of shallow ground, found almost everywhere.
options: It is the other way round.
A heat pump uses electricity to run.
Right: very different temperatures needed.
Heat pumps work far from plate boundaries.

items.q: A school district in a region with no hot rock near the surface wants to cut the natural gas it burns for heating. Propose a geothermal solution and explain how it works.

why.correct: A ground source heat pump fits because it uses the ground's steady shallow temperature, which exists almost everywhere.

specific.frame: The district should install ___, which works because ___.

tech.label: Technology
options: ground source heat pumps
a geothermal power plant
deeper natural gas wells

why.1: A power plant needs hot rock near the surface, which this region lacks.
why.2: More gas wells would not reduce gas burning.

how.label: How it works
options: buried pipes pick up heat from the ground, which stays about the same temperature all year, and the pump moves it into the buildings
the pipes burn gas more efficiently underground
the pipes collect sunlight stored in the soil

why.1: A heat pump burns no gas.
why.2: Shallow ground temperature is steady because the ground stores heat; the system does not collect sunlight directly.

specific.model: The district should install ground source heat pumps, which works because buried pipes pick up heat from the ground, which stays about the same temperature all year, and the pumps move that heat into the schools instead of burning natural gas.

items.q: Which is an advantage of geothermal power plants over wind and solar?
options: Steady output in any weather, day or night
They can be built on any piece of land in the world
They release no gases or dissolved minerals of any kind
They need no drilling or pumping in order to operate

why.correct: Geothermal heat is always there, so plants run around the clock. They are limited to suitable sites and can release some gases.
options: Right: steady, weather-independent output.
They need hot rock near the surface, found in few places.
Steam can carry hydrogen sulfide and dissolved minerals.
Wells must be drilled and water pumped and reinjected.
